passages.title: A simulation, not a deployment
passages.text: TraffiX is a multi-agent traffic-control simulation of six signalised junctions (J1–J6) on the real OpenStreetMap streets of central Tunis, built on Eclipse SUMO and driven through TraCI. It is not deployed on any street: road demand is synthetic and nothing in the project is deployment evidence.
passages.context: ESPRIT 4DS course project, Intelligent Multi-Agent Traffic Management (team of six).
limitations: Simulation only. Road demand is synthetic; emissions are proxies, not measured air quality.

passages.title: One writer per light, a reason for every decision
passages.text: Only one controller per traffic light may change it, a supermaster coordinates the junctions, and every decision is logged with a reason code. A language layer, Synapse, explains decisions from that log and never acts on the simulation.
passages.context: Architecture adopted by the team from aymenhamzik/traffix3.
limitations: The agent architecture was adopted from aymenhamzik/traffix3, not designed by me alone.

passages.title: My part of the team
passages.text: I worked in the Control pair with Fares Ben Kacem, covering SUMO, observations, the A1 agent, safety and the controllers. Pairs build, test and demo each work item, and roles rotate.
passages.context: Team of six ESPRIT 4DS students; README section 11.
limitations: Team project of six students; I did not build it alone, and roles rotate, so other pairs also touched these areas.

passages.title: Fewer car greens while people cross
passages.text: With the trained models, about 18 car green phases per run started while pedestrians were crossing, against 331–405 with SUMO's actuated signals (−95%). The number is not zero.
passages.context: Tunis map, mean of seeds 1–3, three scenarios, models and network of 20 October 2026.
limitations: Three seeds and three scenarios; no difference is significant at p < 0.05.
Simulated with synthetic demand; not a safety result for real streets.

passages.title: Pedestrian wait in the morning peak
passages.text: In the morning-peak scenario, mean pedestrian wait was 116.3 s with the trained models against 144.1 s with actuated signals (−19%).
passages.context: One scenario, mean of 3 seeds, 20 October 2026 run.
limitations: One scenario and three seeds; not statistically significant.

passages.title: Ambulances are slower, and that is not explained yet
passages.text: Emergency-vehicle trips were slower with TraffiX: 240.0 s against 213.2 s with actuated signals and 197.0 s with fixed-time signals. The objective was not met, and the cause is not yet known.
passages.context: Emergency scenario, mean of 3 seeds, 20 October 2026 run.
limitations: Possible causes named in the report (preparation horizon, extra car wait, routes) are untested.

passages.title: Mixed results, none significant
passages.text: Against actuated signals, mean car wait fell 11% in the morning peak and 24% in the incident scenario but rose 20% in the emergency scenario; pedestrian wait rose 11% in the incident scenario. None of the paired t-tests is significant at p < 0.05 with three seeds.
passages.context: Validation report §5.3–5.4.
limitations: Three seeds; synthetic demand; 18 of 21 junction roads use unverified lane counts.

passages.title: Known limitations
passages.text: Demand is synthetic, 18 of 21 junction roads use unverified lane counts, it is a course project until December 2026, and the models must be retrained when the road network changes.
passages.context: Validation report §5.5 and README.

passages.title: Which pages should a person review first
passages.text: The FlyRank capstone asks whether same-day performance and content signals can rank webpages for a more useful next-seven-day editorial review queue than a transparent age-plus-visibility rule. It is a prioritisation signal for human review, not a causal estimate of what a refresh does.
passages.context: FlyRank ML internship capstone (ML-11 research paper), pseudonymised internship warehouse.
limitations: Observational, not causal. It does not show that editing a page increases traffic.

passages.title: Precision@50 of 0.94 against 0.76
passages.text: On 1,583 held-out pages from 8 clients the model never saw, a Random Forest put higher-traffic pages in its top 50 with Precision@50 of 0.94, against 0.76 for the fixed baseline. A hit is a page with at least 8 clicks in the following week, the 75th percentile of the training rows.
passages.context: Features from 31 March 2026; outcome = Google Search Console clicks 1–7 April 2026.
limitations: One decision date and one outcome week; observational, not causal.
The internship warehouse is gated, so the result cannot be fully reproduced in public.

passages.title: Clients kept apart, baseline fixed first
passages.text: The baseline was fixed before the label was used. GroupShuffleSplit kept whole clients on one side: 11,802 training rows from 21 clients and 1,583 test rows from 8 unseen clients, with no overlap. The model is a Random Forest with 150 trees, depth 14, minimum leaf 3 and seed 42.
passages.context: Capstone report, method section.
limitations: A grouped split tests transfer to new clients, not performance over time.

passages.title: A deliberate leakage test
passages.text: Leakage checks confirm that April data appears only in the label, every feature row is from 31 March and no identifier is a predictor. A deliberately leaked label feature produced an inflated score and was removed before the honest run.
passages.context: Capstone report, method section.
limitations: The leaked feature was a planted test, not an accidental leak found in production.

passages.title: Error on the count of clicks
passages.text: On the same held-out rows the Random Forest reached R² 0.50 and MAE 2.51 clicks, against R² 0.26 for the calibrated baseline. A separate validation-audit rerun reports R² 0.52, kept apart.
passages.context: Capstone report, results table; held-out mean outcome 3.42 clicks.
limitations: A one-day snapshot misses later demand spikes; clicks are not revenue.

passages.title: Every flag is explained, a person decides
passages.text: Uploaded PDFs and scans pass pre-flight checks, then Docling extraction with a RapidOCR fallback when confidence is low, schema and business validation, and cohort anomaly detection. Each flag carries a rule, severity, explanation and remediation, with sensitive values masked. The system never writes to an HR information system on its own.
passages.context: Local, self-hosted prototype; README architecture section.
limitations: Prototype tested on synthetic sample documents only.

passages.title: What actually runs today
passages.text: The current runtime is a synchronous FastAPI demo with in-memory jobs. Celery, Redis and PostgreSQL appear only in the planned full-stack mode. CSV and Excel files are outside the current OCR contract.
passages.context: README, runtime modes.
limitations: Planned services are not built.

passages.title: OCR accuracy has not been measured
passages.text: OCR accuracy on real HR documents has not been measured. The prototype's checks run on synthetic PDFs and images with deterministic local tests, and one extractor's confidence is fixed at 0.6 until measured confidence is implemented.
passages.context: Live portfolio HR card; system record line 34.
limitations: No accuracy figure exists for this project.

passages.title: The weakest measured results
passages.text: No project is ranked worst, because the three are measured in different ways. The weakest measured result is TraffiX in the emergency scenario: ambulance trips took 240.0 s against 213.2 s with actuated signals. The HR prototype has no accuracy figure at all, so nothing can be said about it either way. FlyRank beat its baseline on clients the model never saw (Precision@50 0.94 against 0.76), on one decision date.
passages.context: Restates the TraffiX validation report, the HR README and the FlyRank notebook output.
limitations: The three projects use different metrics and conditions, so the numbers are not comparable.
None of the TraffiX differences is significant at p < 0.05 with three seeds.
